defs: Virtual Private Network: an encrypted/secured tunnel across an untrusted or shared network.

course.learn: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) creates a protected tunnel across an untrusted network so remote users or sites can communicate securely.
course.why: Without a secure tunnel, traffic crossing public networks may be observed or modified.
course.example: A remote employee authenticates with MFA and establishes an encrypted VPN tunnel to the corporate network.
course.exam: Know remote-access versus site-to-site VPN, strong authentication, split tunneling considerations, logging, and least privilege.

course.learn: Remote access lets users administer or use organizational resources from outside the local network. It should combine strong authentication, secure transport, endpoint requirements, authorization, and monitoring.
course.why: Remote users connect from networks and devices the organization may not fully control.
course.example: An administrator must use MFA, a managed endpoint, VPN/ZTNA, and a jump host before reaching production servers.
course.exam: CompTIA often favors MFA, least privilege, secure tunneling, endpoint compliance, logging, and limited administrative exposure.

defs: Transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand it.
Transport Layer Security: cryptographic protocol used to protect application communications such as HTTPS.

course.learn: Transport Layer Security (TLS) protects application traffic in transit using authenticated cryptographic negotiation and session encryption. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS.
course.why: TLS protects data from eavesdropping and tampering while it crosses untrusted networks.
course.example: A browser validates a website certificate and negotiates an encrypted TLS session before sending login credentials.
course.exam: TLS is strongly associated with HTTPS and application traffic. Certificate validation matters; “encrypted” is not enough if the peer is not authenticated.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand it.
A suite of protocols that protects IP traffic at the network layer; commonly used for VPNs.

course.learn: IPsec secures IP-layer traffic using protocols that provide integrity, authentication, and optionally confidentiality. It is commonly used for site-to-site or remote-access VPNs.
course.why: Because IPsec operates at the network layer, applications do not need to add their own tunnel logic.
course.example: Two offices build an IPsec tunnel between firewalls so internal subnets communicate securely across the Internet.
course.exam: IPsec = network-layer VPN/security. TLS is more commonly tied to application-layer sessions such as HTTPS.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: SD-WAN centrally controls how branch and wide-area traffic uses multiple links such as broadband, MPLS, or cellular. Policies can choose paths based on application, performance, and security requirements.
course.why: Centralized software control improves flexibility but makes controller security, segmentation, encryption, and policy accuracy important.
course.example: Voice traffic uses the lowest-latency link while general web traffic uses broadband; sensitive traffic is encrypted and segmented by policy.
course.exam: SD-WAN is about software-defined WAN path/control. Secure it with strong management access, encrypted tunnels, segmentation, and monitoring.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Security model that assumes no implicit trust and continuously verifies identities, devices, context, and access requests.
Computing resources delivered on demand from a provider rather than entirely owned and operated locally.
Secure Access Service Edge: cloud-delivered networking and security functions combined around users, identities, and distributed resources.

course.learn: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) combines networking and security services—such as secure web gateway, firewall-as-a-service, CASB, and Zero-Trust access—through cloud-delivered architecture.
course.why: Users and applications may be anywhere, so sending all traffic back through one traditional data-center perimeter can be inefficient and inconsistent.
course.example: A remote user connects to the nearest cloud security point, is evaluated by identity/device policy, and receives access only to approved applications.
course.exam: SASE clues: cloud-delivered networking + security, identity-aware access, distributed users, and Zero Trust alignment.

course.learn: Selecting an effective security control requires matching the control to the threat, asset, architecture, usability needs, scalability, management burden, and evolving risk.
course.why: The strongest theoretical control is not automatically the best if it cannot be deployed, managed, or scaled correctly.
course.example: A small branch may choose a managed cloud security service rather than maintaining several complex appliances locally.
course.exam: Read BEST/MOST questions for constraints such as cost, scalability, ease of management, performance, and required security property.
